title: The Old Bachelor
description: Congreve's first comedy, written while he was still in his early twenties and produced at Drury Lane with a cast that included Betterton and Anne Bracegirdle; it ran for an unprecedented fourteen nights.
plot_or_argument: The old bachelor Bellmour is dissuaded from marriage by his friend Heartwell, who is himself undone by his love for the coquette Sylvia; a series of intrigues, a disguised marriage, and a discovery of true parentage resolve in multiple weddings.
narrative_structure: Five acts of intrigue comedy with a strong comic subplot of Fondlewife, Laetitia, and Vainlove.
principal_characters: Bellmour; Vainlove; Heartwell; Fondlewife; Laetitia; Araminta; Belinda; Sylvia; Bluffe; Lucy
meter_and_prosody: Prose of precocious brilliance; Dryden remarked that the author was 'but a young man' and supplied corrections.
historical_context: Performed at the Theatre Royal, Drury Lane, in January 1693 and published the same year; it was the most successful first play of the decade.
literary_significance: Announced Congreve as the heir to Etherege and Wycherley and launched the last great phase of Restoration comedy.
bibliographical_notes: First published 1693. Standard edition: The Comedies of William Congreve (Derek Hughes, ed., Oxford University Press, 1993); The Complete Plays of William Congreve (Eric S. Rump, ed.).

title: The Double Dealer
description: Congreve's second comedy, a tightly plotted intrigue play built around the double-dealing Maskwell, who betrays his patron, his friends, and his mistresses in pursuit of an heiress.
plot_or_argument: Maskwell, the trusted friend of Mellefont, secretly loves Lady Touchwood and conspires to disinherit Mellefont and win Cynthia; the plot is discovered only at the last moment and the lovers are saved.
narrative_structure: Five acts observing the unities of time and place, a formal experiment in the French manner that made the play less popular than its predecessor.
principal_characters: Maskwell; Mellefont; Lord Touchwood; Lady Touchwood; Cynthia; Lady Froth; Sir Paul Plyant; Careless; Brisk
historical_context: Performed at the Theatre Royal in November 1693 and published in 1694 with a dedicatory epistle to Charles Montagu, later Earl of Halifax.
literary_significance: Congreve's most formally rigorous comedy and one of the most intricate plots in English drama; Maskwell is the finest villain of Restoration comedy.
bibliographical_notes: First published 1694. Standard edition: The Comedies of William Congreve (Derek Hughes, ed., OUP, 1993).

title: Love for Love
description: Congreve's most popular comedy, in which the improvident Valentine, disinherited by his father and pressed by his creditors, feigns madness to escape a forced marriage and finally wins Angelica.
plot_or_argument: Valentine signs away his inheritance to Trapland and Forester; his father Sir Sampson Legend tries to marry him to Miss Prue; the scheming Angelica and the mad prophet Tattle are entangled until the plot resolves in Valentine's recovery and marriage.
narrative_structure: Five acts with a rich comic subplot of the nurse, the astrologer Foresight, and the country Miss Prue.
principal_characters: Valentine; Angelica; Sir Sampson Legend; Ben Legend; Tattle; Mrs Frail; Miss Prue; Foresight; Jeremy; Trapland; Buckram; Scandal
meter_and_prosody: Prose of great variety, from high wit to coarse farce.
historical_context: First performed at the new Lincoln's Inn Fields Theatre on 30 April 1695, the opening of the breakaway actors' company under Betterton, and published the same year.
literary_significance: The most frequently revived of Congreve's comedies in his own lifetime and a principal model for eighteenth-century comedy; its treatment of debt and disinheritance is unusually sharp social commentary.
bibliographical_notes: First published 1695. Standard edition: The Comedies of William Congreve (Derek Hughes, ed., OUP, 1993).

title: The Mourning Bride
description: Congreve's only tragedy, a heroic verse play set in a fictionalised Morocco and Granada, which was the most successful tragedy of the 1690s and the source of the proverbial lines on music and on grief.
plot_or_argument: The Moorish king Manuel keeps Almeria, the widow of his murdered enemy, imprisoned and desires her; a series of disguises, a false death, and the return of the true heir lead to the king's downfall and Almeria's deliverance.
narrative_structure: Five acts in blank verse with a masque and songs.
principal_characters: Almeria; Manuel; Alonzo; Osmyn; Selim; Zara; Heli; Gonzalez
meter_and_prosody: Blank verse, with the famous opening 'Music has charms to soothe a savage breast' and 'Heaven has no rage like love to hatred turned'.
historical_context: Performed at Lincoln's Inn Fields in January 1697 and published in the same year; it ran for thirteen nights, an exceptional success for a tragedy.
literary_significance: The most quoted tragedy of the period and the culmination of the she-tragedy tradition; its sententiae passed into proverbial use.
bibliographical_notes: First published 1697. Standard edition: The Plays of William Congreve (Eric S. Rump, ed., Barnes & Noble, 1962).

title: The Way of the World
description: Congreve's last and greatest comedy, the supreme achievement of the English comedy of manners, in which Mirabell and Millamant negotiate the famous 'proviso' scene and outwit the jealous Lady Wishfort and the treacherous Fainall.
plot_or_argument: Mirabell needs the consent of Lady Wishfort, whose fortune Millamant depends on, and has pretended to court the old lady; Lady Wishfort is enraged when she learns the truth; the villain Fainall tries to seize the estates, and Mirabell defeats him with the deed of trust.
narrative_structure: Five acts of intricate intrigue culminating in the proviso scene (IV.i) and the discovery scene (V), each with a formal balance and symmetry unmatched in English comedy.
principal_characters: Mirabell; Millamant; Lady Wishfort; Fainall; Mrs Fainall; Mrs Marwood; Sir Wilfull Witwoud; Petulant; Waitwell; Foible; Witwoud
meter_and_prosody: Prose of the most refined and musical precision; the proviso scene is the high-water mark of English comic dialogue.
historical_context: Performed at Lincoln's Inn Fields in March 1700 and published the same year; its relative coolness at first performance ended Congreve's dramatic career at the age of thirty.
literary_significance: Universally regarded as the greatest comedy of manners in English and one of the supreme achievements of Restoration literature; it was decisively revalued in the twentieth century by T. S. Eliot and Bonamy Dobrée.
bibliographical_notes: First published 1700. Standard edition: The Comedies of William Congreve (Derek Hughes, ed., OUP, 1993); The Way of the World (Michael Cordner, ed., New Mermaids).

title: The Orphan; or, The Unhappy Marriage
description: Thomas Otway's breakthrough tragedy, in which the orphan Monimia is secretly married to the elder brother Castalio and is tricked into his brother Polydore's bed on the wedding night, destroying them all.
plot_or_argument: Castalio secretly marries Monimia; his brother Polydore, disguised, takes his place in the dark; when the truth emerges, Castalio kills himself in a duel with Polydore and Monimia takes poison.
narrative_structure: Five acts in blank verse, modelled on the domestic tragedy of a wronged woman.
principal_characters: Monimia; Castalio; Polydore; Acasto; Serina; Chaplain; Ernesto
historical_context: Performed at the Duke's Theatre in Dorset Garden in February 1680 and published the same year; Elizabeth Barry's performance as Monimia made her the greatest tragic actress of the age.
literary_significance: The founding work of the 'she-tragedy' mode that dominated Restoration and early eighteenth-century drama, and the play that established Otway's reputation.
bibliographical_notes: First published 1680. Standard edition: The Works of Thomas Otway (Thomas Joannes, ed., 1932); The Orphan (Marianne Novy, ed.).

title: Caius Marius
description: Otway's Roman tragedy, which grafts a Romeo-and-Juliet love story onto the civil wars of Marius and Sulla and was read as a political allegory of the Exclusion Crisis.
plot_or_argument: Young Marius loves Lavinia, the daughter of the Sullan Crassus; the factions' hatred destroys them, and the play ends with Marius's death and Lavinia's.
narrative_structure: Five acts combining Roman history with a Shakespearean love tragedy.
principal_characters: Caius Marius; Young Marius; Lavinia; Sulla; Crassus; Juno; Metellus
meter_and_prosody: Blank verse with a large borrowing from Romeo and Juliet in the balcony scene.
historical_context: Performed at the Duke's Theatre in 1679 during the Exclusion Crisis; the political application was so pointed that the play was suppressed in 1680.
literary_significance: An important document of Whig political drama and of the Restoration use of Roman history as a mirror for contemporary politics.
bibliographical_notes: First published 1680. Standard edition: The Works of Thomas Otway (1932).

title: Venice Preserv'd; or, A Plot Discover'd
description: Otway's masterpiece and the greatest tragedy of the Restoration, in which the young Venetian Jaffeir joins a conspiracy against the Senate to relieve his poverty and is destroyed between his oath to his friends and his love for Belvidera.
plot_or_argument: Jaffeir, disinherited for marrying Belvidera, swears to the conspirators led by Pierre; Belvidera persuades him to betray the plot; the conspirators are condemned, Pierre accuses Jaffeir of treachery, and the two friends die together, Belvidera going mad and dying of grief.
narrative_structure: Five acts in blank verse with a single tragic action of extraordinary intensity and a large role for the hero's female victim.
principal_characters: Jaffeir; Belvidera; Pierre; the Senator Antonio; Priuli; Renault; Spinosa; Theodore; Nadan
meter_and_prosody: Blank verse; the Pierre-Jaffeir friendship scenes are among the most eloquent in Restoration drama.
historical_context: Performed at the Duke's Theatre on 9 February 1682, dedicated to the Duchess of Portsmouth, and read as a Tory attack on Shaftesbury and the Whigs after the Rye House Plot; Antonio caricatures the Whig Earl of Shaftesbury.
literary_significance: The most performed tragedy between Shakespeare's revival and the nineteenth century, and a canonical work of political and emotional tragedy; it profoundly influenced the Romantic poets and remained in repertory until the 1880s.
bibliographical_notes: First published 1682. Standard edition: The Works of Thomas Otway (Thomas Joannes, ed., 1932); Venice Preserv'd (Malcolm Kelsall, ed., New Mermaids).

title: The Forc'd Marriage; or, A Night's Intrigue
description: Aphra Behn's first play, a tragicomedy of forced marriage and intrigue in which Alcander is compelled to marry Erminia while loving another, and the complications are resolved in a set of marriages.
plot_or_argument: The King forces Erminia to marry Alcander, who loves Aminta; disguises and mistaken identities lead to a night of intrigue, and the plot ends with the rightful pairings.
narrative_structure: Five acts of heroic tragicomedy.
principal_characters: Alcander; Erminia; Aminta; Cleontius; Lisander; the King; Galliard
historical_context: Performed at the Duke's Theatre in December 1670 and published in 1671; it ran for six nights, a modest but respectable success for a first play, and by a woman.
literary_significance: The first play by a woman to be performed on the English public stage, marking the beginning of professional female authorship in English drama.
bibliographical_notes: First published 1671. Standard edition: The Works of Aphra Behn (Janet Todd, ed., William Pickering / Ohio State University Press, 1995-6), 7 vols.

title: The Rover; or, The Banish'd Cavaliers
description: Behn's most famous and most successful comedy, set in Naples at carnival time, in which the libertine Rover Willmore pursues the witty Hellena while her sister Florinda evades a forced marriage.
plot_or_argument: At carnival, Hellena disguises herself to meet Willmore; Florinda loves Belvile but is promised to the aged Vincentio and pursued by her brother's friend; a series of attempted rapes, duels, and disguises ends with the marriages of both sisters and Willmore's abandonment by Hellena.
narrative_structure: Five acts of carnival comedy with a strong double plot and a dark undercurrent of sexual violence.
principal_characters: Willmore (the Rover); Hellena; Florinda; Belvile; Blunt; Frederick; Don Pedro; Don Vincentio; Angellica Bianca; Lucetta; Moretta
historical_context: Performed at the Duke's Theatre on 24 March 1677 and dedicated to Charles II's illegitimate son the Earl of Rochester's circle; it derives from Thomas Killigrew's unacted play Thomaso.
literary_significance: The most performed play of the Restoration after The Way of the World and the greatest comedy by a woman before the twentieth century; its treatment of female sexual agency and of carnival liberty is central to modern feminist criticism.
attribution_notes: Attributed to Behn; she acknowledges the debt to Killigrew's Thomaso in the preface.
bibliographical_notes: First published 1677. Standard edition: The Works of Aphra Behn (Janet Todd, ed., 1995-6); The Rover (Anne Russell, ed., Broadview, 2001).

title: The Rover, Part II
description: Behn's sequel, set in London rather than Naples, in which Willmore returns to his roving ways and the same company of cavaliers is caught up in the intrigues of the town.
plot_or_argument: Willmore pursues the coquettes of London while Hellena and the other characters from the first play reappear; the intrigues of the town are resolved with Willmore unchanged.
narrative_structure: Five acts of intrigue comedy.
principal_characters: Willmore; Hellena; Belvile; Blunt; Frederick; Lady Galliard; Cornelia
historical_context: Performed at the Duke's Theatre in 1681 and published in the same year; it was less successful than Part I.
literary_significance: An important sequel that transfers the carnival liberty of Naples to Restoration London and sharpens Behn's satire on the town's treatment of women.
bibliographical_notes: First published 1681. Standard edition: The Works of Aphra Behn (Janet Todd, ed., 1995-6).

title: Abdelazer; or, The Moor's Revenge
description: Behn's revenge tragedy of the Moorish prince Abdelazer, who seduces and destroys the Queen of Spain in a series of murders; it reworks Marston's Lust's Dominion and supplied Purcell with the theme of 'The Prince of Denmark's March'.
plot_or_argument: Abdelazer, the Moorish heir deprived of his throne, seduces the Queen, murders the King, and finally falls; the play is a sustained study of ambition and revenge without remorse.
narrative_structure: Five acts of revenge tragedy with a rapid succession of murders.
principal_characters: Abdelazer; the Queen; the King of Spain; Florella; Osmin; Cardinal; Antonio; Philip
historical_context: Performed at the Duke's Theatre in 1677 and published in the same year; a 1695 revival used Purcell's incidental music.
literary_significance: The most successful of Behn's tragedies and an important rewriting of the early modern Moor-revenge tradition; it influenced later representations of the Moorish villain.
bibliographical_notes: First published 1677. Standard edition: The Works of Aphra Behn (Janet Todd, ed., 1995-6).

title: The Widow Ranter; or, The History of Bacon in Virginia
description: Behn's last play, produced posthumously, a tragicomedy set in colonial Virginia during Bacon's Rebellion of 1676, combining a love intrigue with an unprecedentedly sympathetic treatment of Native Americans.
plot_or_argument: The wealthy tobacco-planting Widow Ranter loves the dashing Dareing; Bacon leads a rebellion against the colonial government to defend the settlers from Indian attacks; Bacon falls in love with the Indian queen Semernia, kills her accidentally, and dies, while the comic plot resolves in marriage.
narrative_structure: Five acts with a tragic historical plot and a comic plantation plot set in the same Virginian world.
principal_characters: the Widow Ranter; Dareing; Nathaniel Bacon; Semernia; Caverno; Hazard; Friendly; Chrisante; Flora
historical_context: Written c. 1688-9, produced at the Theatre Royal in November 1689, and published posthumously in 1690 with a preface by an unknown hand.
literary_significance: The first English play set in colonial America and one of the earliest literary treatments of the Atlantic slave economy and of Anglo-Indian relations; it has become central to postcolonial readings of Restoration drama.
bibliographical_notes: First published 1690. Standard edition: The Works of Aphra Behn (Janet Todd, ed., 1995-6); The Widow Ranter (Paula R. Backscheider, ed., Broadview, 2011).

title: Love-Letters Between a Nobleman and His Sister
description: Behn's epistolary novel in three parts, based on the real scandal of Lord Grey of Warke's elopement with his wife's sister, in which Philander seduces Silvia and she descends through a series of lovers into prostitution and political intrigue.
plot_or_argument: Philander writes to Silvia, his sister-in-law; they elope; he tires of her and takes another mistress; Silvia responds by seducing and abandoning a series of men, becoming a courtesan and finally a political agent of Monmouth's rebellion.
narrative_structure: Three parts (1684, 1685, 1687) of letters with narrative interludes, the first substantial English epistolary fiction.
principal_characters: Philander; Silvia; Calista; Octavio; Don Alonzo; Cesario; the Countess
historical_context: Published in three parts between 1684 and 1687, at the time of the Monmouth Rebellion; it is a roman à clef on the Grey-Sisters scandal.
literary_significance: The first major English epistolary novel and a decisive step toward the eighteenth-century novel of Richardson and Laclos; its portrayal of a woman's sexual and political agency was unprecedented.
attribution_notes: Published anonymously in parts; attribution to Behn is long-established and undisputed.
bibliographical_notes: First published 1684-7 in three parts. Standard edition: The Works of Aphra Behn, vol. II (Janet Todd, ed., 1995); Love-Letters Between a Nobleman and His Sister (Janet Todd, ed., Penguin Classics, 1996).

title: Oroonoko; or, The Royal Slave (Behn)
description: Behn's short novel, narrated by a female traveller in the English colony of Surinam, on the African prince Oroonoko, who is sold into slavery, leads a failed revolt, and is barbarously executed; it is the founding text of English anti-slavery fiction.
plot_or_argument: Oroonoko, grandson of the king of Coramantien, loves Imoinda; both are sold into slavery and reunited in Surinam; he leads an unsuccessful rebellion, is captured, promises peace, is whipped and dismembered, and kills his pregnant wife before his own execution.
narrative_structure: A first-person frame narrative with the narrator's eyewitness account, digressions on Surinam's flora, fauna, and indigenous people, and a sustained portrait of Oroonoko as a European-style hero.
principal_characters: Oroonoko; Imoinda; the narrator; Caesar; Trefry; Byam; Banister; the Indian lovers
meter_and_prosody: Elegant Restoration prose combining travel description with tragic narrative.
historical_context: Published in 1688, the year of the Revolution and of Behn's death; it draws on her claimed residence in Surinam in 1663-4.
literary_significance: The most influential prose fiction of the Restoration; it established the 'noble savage' trope, initiated the English anti-slavery literary tradition, and has become a canonical text of early modern women's writing and of postcolonial criticism. Thomas Southerne's 1695 stage adaptation held the stage for over a century.
attribution_notes: Attributed to Behn; the narrator's identity is a literary persona, though the Surinam material is generally accepted as drawing on her experience.
bibliographical_notes: First published 1688. Standard edition: Oroonoko (Joanna Lipking, ed., Norton Critical Editions, 2011); The Works of Aphra Behn, vol. III (Janet Todd, ed., 1995).

title: The Fair Jilt; or, The Amours of Prince Tarquin and Sister Henrietta
description: Behn's short prose fiction based on the real scandal of Sister Henrietta of the Convent of the Holy Sepulchre at Antwerp, who was tried for attempting to murder her sister; Behn, who sat on the jury, presents her as a beautiful and irresistible temptress.
plot_or_argument: The beautiful Henrietta, forced into a convent, is pursued by the friar Tarquin; her intrigues with a nobleman and her attempt to murder her sister lead to her trial, and she is finally reconciled to the church.
narrative_structure: A short prose narrative with a documentary frame, presented as a true history.
principal_characters: Sister Henrietta; Prince Tarquin; the Prince of Antwerp; the Prioress
meter_and_prosody: Restoration prose of the scandal-chronicle type.
historical_context: Published in 1688; Behn claimed to have witnessed the events while in the Spanish Netherlands in the 1680s.
literary_significance: An important example of the Restoration scandal narrative and of Behn's exploitation of the boundary between reportage and fiction.
bibliographical_notes: First published 1688. Standard edition: The Works of Aphra Behn, vol. III (Janet Todd, ed., 1995).

title: Poems upon Several Occasions with a Voyage to the Island of Love (Behn)
description: Behn's collected verse, including her celebrated lyric 'The Disappointment', the Pindaric odes to political occasions, and the translation of Fontenelle's Voyage to the Island of Love.
plot_or_argument: The volume gathers court odes, love lyrics, songs, elegies, and political verse, including the Whig odes to Monmouth and the Tory poems of the 1680s.
narrative_structure: A poetical miscellany with an appended translation of Fontenelle.
meter_and_prosody: Varied: Pindaric odes, heroic couplets, song stanzas.
historical_context: Published in 1684 by Tonson, establishing Behn as the first English woman to earn a living by her pen; a second volume appeared posthumously in 1701.
literary_significance: The most important collection of poetry by an English woman before the eighteenth century; 'The Disappointment' is a canonical treatment of female sexual experience and its failure.
bibliographical_notes: First published 1684; Poems upon Several Occasions, with A Voyage to the Island of Love (1684) and A Miscellany of Poems (1701). Standard edition: The Works of Aphra Behn, vol. I (Janet Todd, ed., 1995).

title: The Fatal Marriage; or, The Innocent Adultery
description: Thomas Southerne's most successful tragedy, an adaptation of two of Behn's novellas, in which Isabella, believing her husband Alonzo dead, remarries and is destroyed when the first husband returns.
plot_or_argument: Isabella, in poverty, believes Alonzo dead and marries Biron; Alonzo returns; Isabella, unable to bear the guilt, kills Biron's brother and then herself.
narrative_structure: Five acts in blank verse with a subordinate comic plot.
principal_characters: Isabella; Alonzo; Biron; Baldwin; Carlos; Anne
historical_context: Performed at the Theatre Royal in 1694 and published the same year; Elizabeth Barry's Isabella was one of the great performances of the age, and the play held the stage into the nineteenth century.
literary_significance: The most popular she-tragedy of the 1690s and an important adaptation of Behn's prose fiction for the stage.
attribution_notes: Attributed to Southerne; he acknowledges the debt to Behn in the dedication.
bibliographical_notes: First published 1694. Standard edition: The Plays of Thomas Southerne (Robert Jordan and Eugene H. Hughes, eds., 1988).

title: Oroonoko (Southerne's adaptation)
description: Southerne's stage version of Behn's novella, which added a comic subplot of two London ladies and made Oroonoko the standard tragic role of the eighteenth century.
plot_or_argument: Oroonoko, sold into slavery in Surinam, is reunited with Imoinda; he leads a failed revolt; the lieutenant-governor betrays him; Imoinda kills herself and Oroonoko is executed.
narrative_structure: Five acts in blank verse with a substantial comic subplot and a large sentimental role for the hero.
principal_characters: Oroonoko; Imoinda; Aboan; Charlotte; the Lieutenant-Governor; Widow Lackitt; Welldon; Blandford
meter_and_prosody: Blank verse with prose in the comic plot.
historical_context: Performed at Lincoln's Inn Fields in 1695 and published in 1696; it was the most frequently performed tragedy of the eighteenth century after Shakespeare and Otway.
literary_significance: The adaptation that made Oroonoko a canonical stage figure and that spread Behn's story, and the issue of slavery, to eighteenth-century audiences across Britain and America.
attribution_notes: Attributed to Southerne; his prologue acknowledges Behn as the source.
bibliographical_notes: First published 1696. Standard edition: The Plays of Thomas Southerne (1988); Oroonoko adaptations (Maximilian E. Novak and George A. Guffey, eds., 1975).

title: The Relapse; or, Virtue in Danger
description: Vanbrugh's first comedy, written as an answer to Cibber's reformed Love's Last Shift, in which the rake Loveless relapses into adultery and the fop Lord Foppington is cheated of his bride.
plot_or_argument: Loveless, briefly reformed by Cibber's Amanda, seduces Berinthia; Lord Foppington is tricked out of his fiancée Miss Hoyden by his brother Sir Tunbelly's gullibility; the play ends without moral resolution.
narrative_structure: Five acts with two parallel plots and a deliberate refusal of the reform ending.
principal_characters: Loveless; Berinthia; Amanda; Lord Foppington; Young Fashion; Miss Hoyden; Sir Tunbelly Clumsey; Nurse; Bull
historical_context: Performed at Drury Lane on 21 November 1696 and published in 1697; it was an immediate success and made Vanbrugh's reputation.
literary_significance: One of the last great Restoration comedies and the target of the moral reformers Collier and Dennis; Lord Foppington became the standard eighteenth-century fop.
bibliographical_notes: First published 1697. Standard edition: The Plays of Sir John Vanbrugh (Michael Cordner, ed., Oxford University Press, 1991).

title: The Provoked Wife
description: Vanbrugh's second comedy, a dark and daring treatment of a brutal marriage, in which Lady Brute endures her husband's drunken abuse and the question of divorce and remarriage is openly debated.
plot_or_argument: Sir John Brute beats and humiliates his wife; she is courted by Constant, her husband's nephew; the play debates whether a woman may lawfully leave a cruel husband and ends ambiguously with no resolution of the marriage.
narrative_structure: Five acts with a comic subplot of the fop Colonel Bully and the disguise scenes in the tavern.
principal_characters: Sir John Brute; Lady Brute; Constant; Heartfree; Belinda; Lady Fanciful; Colonel Bully; Mademoiselle
historical_context: Performed at Lincoln's Inn Fields in May 1697 and published the same year; the ecclesiastical courts' handling of marriage separation was a live issue, and the play provoked Jeremy Collier's attack in A Short View of the Immorality of the English Stage (1698).
literary_significance: The most serious and most controversial of the Restoration comedies; its treatment of marital cruelty and female agency makes it a central text for feminist readings of the period.
bibliographical_notes: First published 1697. Standard edition: The Plays of Sir John Vanbrugh (Michael Cordner, ed., OUP, 1991).

title: Love and a Bottle
description: Farquhar's first comedy, a lively if derivative play of intrigue in which the Irish adventurer Roebuck arrives in London with nothing but love and a bottle and sets about marrying an heiress.
plot_or_argument: Roebuck, newly arrived from Ireland, pursues the heiress Lucinda while his servant and the town's rogues complicate the plot; the intrigue is resolved in marriage.
narrative_structure: Five acts of intrigue comedy.
principal_characters: Roebuck; Lucinda; Leanwell; Clear; Sabina; Mrs Gainall; Lyrick
historical_context: Performed at Drury Lane in 1698 and published in 1699; Farquhar was a young Irish actor turned playwright after a stage accident.
literary_significance: The debut of the last important Restoration dramatist and the beginning of the transition from the comedy of manners to the sentimental comedy of the eighteenth century.
bibliographical_notes: First published 1699. Standard edition: The Works of George Farquhar (Shirley Strum Kenny, ed., Clarendon Press, 1988).

title: The Constant Couple; or, A Trip to the Jubilee
description: Farquhar's second and most popular comedy, in which the gay, generous Sir Harry Wildair returns from Paris and wins the virtuous Angelica; the character became the signature role of Robert Wilks.
plot_or_argument: Sir Harry Wildair, a rake with a good heart, returns to London during the Jubilee year; he is courted by Lady Lurewell and falls for the disguised Angelica; the plot resolves in marriage and reformation without sentimentality.
narrative_structure: Five acts with a double plot of high intrigue and low comic theft.
principal_characters: Sir Harry Wildair; Lady Lurewell; Angelica; Standard; Colonel Standard; Vizard; Smuggler; Dapper; Tom Errand
historical_context: Performed at Drury Lane in November 1699 and published in 1700; the sequel Sir Harry Wildair followed in 1701.
literary_significance: One of the most popular plays of the early eighteenth century and the creation of the good-hearted rake that anticipated the sentimental hero; it marks Farquhar's decisive break with Restoration cynicism.
bibliographical_notes: First published 1700. Standard edition: The Works of George Farquhar (Shirley Strum Kenny, ed., Clarendon Press, 1988).

title: The Recruiting Officer
description: Farquhar's comedy of military recruiting in the provincial town of Shrewsbury, drawn from his own experience as a recruiting officer in Ireland during the War of the Spanish Succession.
plot_or_argument: Captains Plume and Brazen recruit soldiers and lovers in Shrewsbury; Plume courts the heiress Silvia, who disguises herself as a country boy to follow him; the plot resolves in marriage and enlistment.
narrative_structure: Five acts with a strong comic subplot of the justices Balance and Worthy and the recruiting sergeant Kite.
principal_characters: Captain Plume; Silvia; Sergeant Kite; Captain Brazen; Justice Balance; Melinda; Lucy; Rose
historical_context: Performed at Drury Lane in April 1706 and published the same year; it was the most successful new play of the season.
literary_significance: The most frequently revived comedy of the eighteenth century and one of the first plays to make provincial English life its setting; it is the direct ancestor of Goldsmith's She Stoops to Conquer.
bibliographical_notes: First published 1706. Standard edition: The Works of George Farquhar (Shirley Strum Kenny, ed., Clarendon Press, 1988); The Recruiting Officer (John Barnard, ed., New Mermaids).

title: The Beaux' Stratagem
description: Farquhar's last and greatest comedy, written on his deathbed, in which the fortune-hunters Archer and Aimwell arrive at Lichfield to repair their ruined estates and encounter the unhappily married Mrs Sullen.
plot_or_argument: Archer and Aimwell take turns posing as lord and servant at Lichfield; Aimwell courts Dorinda, Archer is drawn into the unhappy marriage of Mrs Sullen and Sullen; a highway robbery, a French invasion scare, and the discovery that Aimwell is not the real lord resolve the plot in marriage and reconciliation.
narrative_structure: Five acts with the celebrated bedroom scene (III.iii) in which Archer and Mrs Sullen debate marriage and divorce.
principal_characters: Archer; Aimwell; Mrs Sullen; Sullen; Dorinda; Lady Bountiful; Cherry; Boniface; Gibbet; Count Bellairde; Foigard
meter_and_prosody: Prose of remarkable richness and speed.
historical_context: Performed at the Queen's Theatre in the Haymarket on 8 March 1707 and published the same year; Farquhar died in March or April 1707, weeks after the first performance.
literary_significance: The finest comedy of the early eighteenth century and the culmination of the Restoration tradition; its treatment of divorce and of provincial English society was ahead of its time, and it has been continuously revived since.
bibliographical_notes: First published 1707. Standard edition: The Works of George Farquhar (Shirley Strum Kenny, ed., Clarendon Press, 1988); The Beaux' Stratagem (Michael Scott, ed., New Mermaids).

title: Love's Last Shift; or, The Fool in Fashion
description: Colley Cibber's first comedy, in which the rake Loveless is reformed by his long-suffering wife Amanda; the play's famous double structure — libertine comedy in the first half, moral reform in the second — provoked Vanbrugh's answer in The Relapse.
plot_or_argument: Loveless, believing Amanda a stranger, seduces her in disguise; she reveals herself and he is reformed; the comic subplot of Sir Novelty Fashion satirises the fashionable fop.
narrative_structure: Five acts with a sharp generic shift at the centre that critics have called the origin of sentimental comedy.
principal_characters: Loveless; Amanda; Sir Novelty Fashion; Young Worthy; Snap; Narcissa; Flareit
historical_context: Performed at Drury Lane in January 1696 with Cibber himself as Sir Novelty Fashion; the role made him famous and the play was a great success.
literary_significance: Usually cited as the first sentimental comedy in English and the pivot between Restoration libertinism and eighteenth-century moral reform; Cibber's career as actor-manager of Drury Lane shaped the Georgian stage.
bibliographical_notes: First published 1696. Standard edition: The Plays of Colley Cibber (John Wilson Hooke, ed., 1939).
